chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan ibn Yahya and Ibn Abi Umayr from Rifa'ah ibn Musa said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a stomach ailment and severe pain: does he enter Mecca in a state of non-pilgrim (halal)? He said, 'He does not enter it except as a pilgrim (muhrim).' And he said, 'They grant him exemption (from the obligation of entering in the state of ihram); indeed, the woodcutters and the gatherers came to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) and asked him, so he permitted them to enter in a state of halal.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What this report contains regarding the patient not entering it except as a pilgrim is according to preference (afdal) and priority (awla), and it is permissible for him to leave it (the obligation) according to what we have previously stated. As for the report that he narrated:

key_terms.حَلَالًا: In a state of non-pilgrim (not in Ihram)
key_terms.مُحْرِمًا: In the state of Ihram (pilgrimal state)
key_terms.يُحْرِمُونَ عَنْهُ: They grant him exemption from the obligation of Ihram

ai.seo_question: Does a sick person need to enter Mecca in the state of Ihram for Hajj?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi clarifies that the exemption for the sick to enter Mecca in a state of Halal is a concession (rukhsa) rather than a strict obligation, making it preferable but not mandatory to perform Ihram. This ruling is grounded in the precedent of the Prophet (SAW) granting similar exemptions to woodcutters and gatherers who entered for specific needs, establishing a principle of ease for those with valid excuses. The narration highlights the flexibility in Shia fiqh regarding the entry conditions for Hajj and Umrah when health impediments exist.
